title: Fierce and kind: Shankara
hook: the wild god drinks the poison no one else can touch, and his gentlest name is Shankara
carry: shiva's fierceness is for our well-being
tomorrow: who ties the soul, and who unties it?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Shiva Sahasranama opened: one god, many names, and Sthanu, the steady post. Today, a fierce god's gentle names.
screen: `ONE GOD, MANY NAMES.` · `TODAY: TWO GENTLE NAMES.`

segments.voice: What do you call someone who frightens people and is still the one they run to? Shiva sits in cremation grounds, smeared with ash, a snake around his neck. Yesterday's list held Bhima, the fearsome one. And yet, in the bhajans sung at temples and in living rooms, the names you'll hear most are soft ones. Shambho. Shankara. Two names from the same hymn, and they don't sound frightening at all.
screen: `FEARSOME, AND STILL RUN TO.` → `SHAMBHO. SHANKARA.` → `THE GENTLE NAMES.`

segments.voice: Start with a story told to Hindu children everywhere. The gods and the demons churned the ocean of milk for the nectar of immortality. But before any treasure came up, out rose a poison so deadly it began to burn the worlds. Everyone ran. Everyone except Shiva, the wild one from the cremation grounds. He took the poison and drank it. In many tellings Parvati caught his throat so it wouldn't go down, and it stayed there and turned his throat blue. That's why one of his names is Nilakantha, the blue-throated. The fearsome one was the only one who could hold the harm. Now hear two of his names. Shankara: tradition explains it as the one who makes well-being, from sham, ease, and kara, the maker. Shambhu: the one from whom well-being comes. A Vedic hymn still chanted in temples, the Shri Rudram, keeps the same pattern. It opens by bowing to Rudra's anger and his arrows, not pretending he's harmless. Deep in the hymn it turns, and bows to him as Shambhu, as Shankara, as Shiva, the auspicious one. That's where the words namah shivaya are heard. So when the sahasranama puts Bhima, the fearsome, beside Shankara, it isn't confused. This is the teaching: in Hindu devotion, Shiva's fierceness is for well-being. He burns what harms and swallows what would poison. So when a family in a hospital waiting room quietly chants to Shiva, they aren't asking a frightening god to stay away. They're calling Shankara, the one who drank the poison so others wouldn't have to.
screen: `THE CHURNING OF THE OCEAN.` · `SHIVA DRINKS THE POISON: NILAKANTHA.` · `SHANKARA: THE MAKER OF WELL-BEING.` · `THE RUDRAM: FROM ANGER TO NAMAH SHIVAYA.` · then, large: `HIS FIERCENESS IS FOR WELL-BEING.`

segments.voice: Sit tall and breathe out slowly. If you pray, say Om Namah Shivaya on each out-breath, the words heard in the Rudram, five or eleven times, picturing the blue throat that held the world's poison. If you don't, bring to mind one fierce person in your life, and on each out-breath, name one thing their fierceness has protected.
The Shiva Sahasranama. Today's names from it: Shankara, the one who makes well-being, and Shambhu, from whom well-being comes. And the story behind them: Nilakantha, the blue-throated one.
Your line: Shiva's fierceness is for our well-being. The blue throat shows it. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1133 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHO TIES THE SOUL, AND WHO UNTIES IT?`

howItsDone: Devotees greet Shiva with names like Shambho, Shankara and Nilakantha in songs and chants; the Shri Rudram, with its line namah shivaya, is chanted in Shiva temples, especially during abhisheka, and Om Namah Shivaya is repeated as a mantra.

notes: Selection two of seven. Glosses: Shankara 'the one who makes well-being' (sham + kara) and Shambhu 'the one from whom well-being comes', presented as 'usually explained'. These follow standard lexicons (Monier-Williams). Confirm both are in the Mahabharata list and the glosses.

Shri Rudram: opening bows to Rudra's anger and arrows ('namaste rudra manyava ...'); the eighth section bows to Shambhu, Shankara, Shiva and 'shivatara' (the more auspicious), where 'namah shivaya' occurs. Paraphrased. Confirm, and confirm Taittiriya Samhita 4.5 as the reference.
'These names are older than any sahasranama' rests on the Rudram being Vedic. A Keeper may prefer softer phrasing.
'Many people know this from their own lives' is about the listener's experience, not a claim about a tradition's members; check tone.
